title: Analyzing Literary Texts
description: Analyze literary texts for plot, character, theme, and author's craft.
objectives: Analyze how plot elements develop theme

lessons.title: Plot and Theme
lessons.content: Plot events are chosen deliberately to develop theme.
examples: Conflict drives the protagonist toward change — that change reveals theme
Rising action builds tension; the climax is the turning point

lessons.title: Character Analysis
lessons.content: Examine what characters say, do, think, and how others react to them.
examples: Direct characterization: 'She was ruthlessly ambitious'
Indirect: show through dialogue, actions, others' reactions

title: Argument and Evidence
description: Identify and evaluate arguments in informational texts.
objectives: Evaluate the relevance and sufficiency of evidence

lessons.title: Argument Structure
lessons.content: An argument has a claim (position) supported by reasons and evidence.
examples: Claim: 'Social media is harmful to teens'
Reason: 'It increases anxiety'
Evidence: 'Studies show teens who use social media 3+ hours/day are 60% more likely to report depression'

lessons.title: Evaluating Evidence
lessons.content: Ask: Is evidence relevant? Sufficient? Credible?
examples: One anecdote does not prove a trend
Statistics from peer-reviewed studies are stronger than personal opinions

title: Vocabulary in Context
description: Determine word meaning from context; study word relationships.
objectives: Use context clues to infer word meaning

lessons.title: Context Clues
lessons.content: Words and sentences surrounding an unknown word can help you infer its meaning.
examples: 'The arid, bone-dry desert offered no water' → arid = dry
'She was obstinate — no matter what we said, she refused to change' → obstinate = stubborn

lessons.title: Connotation
lessons.content: Words have literal meanings (denotation) and emotional associations (connotation).
examples: Slender (positive) vs. scrawny (negative) — both mean thin
Assertive (positive) vs. aggressive (negative) — similar actions, different implications

title: Informational Writing — Research Essay
description: Plan and write a researched informational essay with proper citations.
objectives: Write with proper citations (MLA basic format)

lessons.title: Research Process
lessons.content: Good research essays go through stages: question → sources → notes → draft → revise.
examples: Narrow your topic: not 'climate change' but 'how climate change affects coral reefs'
Use 3+ sources; look for consensus among credible sources

lessons.title: Citations
lessons.content: Give credit to sources within the text and in a works cited list.
examples: In-text: (National Geographic, 2022)
Works cited: Author Last, First. 'Article Title.' Source, Date.

title: Narrative Writing
description: Write a narrative with a well-developed plot, vivid description, and authentic dialogue.
objectives: Use narrative techniques: pacing, description, dialogue
Establish a clear conflict and resolution
Write with a consistent point of view

lessons.title: Narrative Techniques
lessons.content: Strong narrative writing uses specific techniques to engage readers.
examples: Show, don't tell: 'Her hands trembled as she reached for the envelope' (not: 'She was nervous')
Pacing: slow down during important scenes; speed up through transitions
Dialogue reveals character and advances plot

lessons.title: Strong Beginnings
lessons.content: The opening line should hook the reader immediately.
examples: In medias res: begin in the middle of action
Intriguing question or statement
Vivid description that sets the scene

title: Grammar — Complex Sentences
description: Write and punctuate complex sentences using subordinating conjunctions.

lessons.title: Complex Sentences
lessons.content: A complex sentence has one independent clause and at least one dependent clause.
examples: 'Although it was raining, we played outside.' (dependent clause first → comma)
'We played outside although it was raining.' (independent first → no comma)
Subordinating conjunctions: although, because, since, while, unless, whenever

title: Reading Poetry — Analyzing Sound and Meaning
description: Analyze how sound devices and structure contribute to a poem's meaning.
objectives: Analyze the effect of rhyme and rhythm
Interpret the meaning of a poem

lessons.title: Sound Devices
lessons.content: Poets use sound to create mood and reinforce meaning.
examples: Alliteration: 'Peter Piper picked a peck of pickled peppers'
Assonance: 'The rain in Spain stays mainly in the plain' (long 'a' sounds)
Consonance: 'the luck of the duck in the muck'

lessons.title: Close Reading of Poetry
lessons.content: Read a poem multiple times; each reading reveals more.
examples: First read: overall impression
Second read: identify structure, rhyme, sound devices
Third read: connect structure to meaning

title: Media Literacy
description: Analyze how media presents information and shapes perception.
objectives: Identify purpose and audience of media

lessons.title: Media Purpose
lessons.content: Every media message has a purpose: inform, persuade, entertain, or sell.
examples: News article: inform (ideally objective)
Advertisement: persuade and sell
Satirical news: entertain while commenting on current events

lessons.title: Evaluating Sources — SIFT
lessons.content: SIFT method: Stop, Investigate, Find better coverage, Trace claims.
examples: Stop before sharing — check if it's credible
Investigate the source: who created it and why?
Find other sources covering the same story
Trace quotes to originals to check context

title: Shakespeare Introduction
description: Introduction to Shakespeare's language, themes, and historical context.
objectives: Understand basic facts about Shakespeare and his era
Analyze a scene for character and theme

lessons.title: Shakespeare's World
lessons.content: Shakespeare wrote in Elizabethan England during a cultural golden age.
examples: Born in Stratford-upon-Avon, 1564; died 1616
Wrote 37 plays and 154 sonnets
The Globe Theatre: outdoor amphitheater; audiences stood or sat around the stage

lessons.title: Reading Shakespeare
lessons.content: Break down thee/thou/dost language; use the context to infer meaning.
examples: 'Thou' = you (informal), 'thee' = you (object)
'Dost' = do/does: 'What dost thou think?' = 'What do you think?'
Read for meaning first, then worry about every word

title: Speaking and Listening — Presentations
description: Plan and deliver an organized oral presentation with visual support.
objectives: Organize a presentation with a clear structure
Use evidence and visual aids effectively

lessons.title: Organizing a Presentation
lessons.content: Structure: hook → main points (2-3) → conclusion. Each point needs evidence.
examples: Opening hook: striking statistic, question, or story
Each slide should have one main idea with minimal text
End with a memorable takeaway or call to action

lessons.title: Delivery Techniques
lessons.content: How you say it matters as much as what you say.
examples: Maintain eye contact with the audience (not the screen)
Vary pace and volume for emphasis
Practice enough times that you don't need to read from notes
